questions.q: By default, what two independent limits determine when Kafka deletes old data from a topic?
options: Time-based (log.retention.hours) and size-based (log.retention.bytes) — whichever is hit first triggers deletion
Only the number of consumers currently subscribed
Only the total number of partitions in the topic
Kafka never deletes data unless a human manually triggers it
questions.explain: Both limits can be set at once, and whichever threshold a partition reaches first is the one that triggers deletion.

questions.q: What could cause size-based deletion to trigger well before a generous time-based limit is reached?
options: A sudden burst of unusually high message volume filling the size limit faster than expected
Kafka ignores log.retention.bytes whenever log.retention.hours is also set
Size-based retention only applies to compacted topics
It is impossible for size-based deletion to trigger before time-based deletion
questions.explain: The two limits are independent — a volume spike can hit the byte ceiling long before the configured hours elapse.

questions.q: How does a compacted topic (cleanup.policy=compact) fundamentally differ from time- or size-based retention, per this lesson?
options: It keeps the latest value for every key forever, deleting only the older superseded values for that key — not a longer retention window
It is simply time-based retention with a longer default window
It deletes all data for a key as soon as a new value for that key arrives
It disables retention entirely, keeping every historical value for every key forever
questions.explain: Compaction is a genuinely different model — it answers "what's the current state," not "how much history to keep."

questions.q: According to this lesson, why would cleanup.policy=compact be the wrong choice for an order-history topic where every past order matters?
options: Because compaction deletes older superseded values for a key, so earlier orders for the same customer key would be lost
Because compacted topics cannot be read by consumers at all
Because compaction only works with JSON, never Avro
Because compacted topics have no partition leader
questions.explain: Compaction is built for "latest value per key" use cases like a changelog — not for histories where every past event needs to survive.

questions.q: What question does time- and size-based retention answer, versus what question compaction answers, per this lesson?
options: Time/size retention answers "how much history to keep"; compaction answers "what does the current state look like right now"
Both answer exactly the same question in different units
Time/size retention answers "what does the current state look like"; compaction answers "how much history to keep"
Neither retention model answers any meaningful question about data lifecycle
questions.explain: That distinction is the core point of this lesson — they're not interchangeable settings for the same goal.
